title: The first isomorphism theorem
objectives: Prove the first isomorphism theorem and use it to identify a quotient.

screens.title: Three times, on a clock
screens.prose: Take $\varphi(x) = 3x$ on $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$, a homomorphism (l10). The grid shows $3x \bmod 12$ for $x = 0$ to $3$. Fill in the rest; each value appears in the grid as you type.
screens.question: Fill in $3x \bmod 12$ for $x = 4$ to $11$.

hints.text: Multiply by 3, then take away 12 as often as you can.
$3 \times 4 = 12 \equiv 0$ and $3 \times 5 = 15 \equiv 3$.
The values repeat 0, 3, 6, 9 every four inputs.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Reduce each product modulo 12.

byKey.r0c1: You wrote 12 for $x = 4$. In $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$, 12 is the same element as 0.

explain.text: $3x \bmod 12$ runs 0, 3, 6, 9 and then repeats. So each value is hit by three inputs. The image is $\{0, 3, 6, 9\}$.

screens.title: What goes to zero
screens.prose: Now the whole row is filled in. The kernel of $\varphi$ is the set of inputs sent to 0.
screens.question: Tap every input that $3x$ sends to 0.

hints.text: Look for the cells holding 0.
There are three of them, four apart.
Inputs 0, 4 and 8.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap only the inputs whose cell reads 0.

explain.text: $3x \equiv 0 \pmod{12}$ exactly when 4 divides $x$. So the kernel is $\{0, 4, 8\}$. It has 3 elements, and 3 inputs land on each value.

screens.title: One coset per value
screens.prose: Sort the inputs by value. Each row is a coset $x + K$ of $K = \{0, 4, 8\}$, and it goes to one value. This is the **first isomorphism theorem**: for a homomorphism $\varphi : G \to H$, $G/\ker\varphi \cong \operatorname{im}\varphi$ by $\psi(gK) = \varphi(g)$. Pinter calls it the fundamental homomorphism theorem.
screens.question: How many elements does $\mathbb{Z}_{12}/K$ have?

hints.text: Count the rows of the grid.
Each row is one coset.
$12 / 3 = 4$ cosets, one per value 0, 3, 6, 9.

feedback.correct: Right. Four cosets match the four values: $\mathbb{Z}_{12}/\{0, 4, 8\} \cong \{0, 3, 6, 9\} \cong \mathbb{Z}_4$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cosets, the rows, not the elements of one row.

byKey.size: You counted the elements of one coset. The quotient's elements are the cosets themselves.

explain.text: The four cosets match the four values, so $12 = 3 \times 4$. In general $|G| = |\ker\varphi| \cdot |\operatorname{im}\varphi|$ for finite $G$. That is the group form of rank-nullity (`linear-maps` l7).

screens.title: Four quotients for free
screens.prose: The theorem turns a kernel and an image into a quotient: $G/\ker\varphi \cong \operatorname{im}\varphi$. The table lists four homomorphisms.
screens.question: Which statements follow from the theorem? Select all that apply.

options.why: You kept only the sign of $\det$. The image is every non-zero real, so the quotient matches $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$.

options.text: $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z} \cong$ the unit circle, from $t \mapsto e^{2\pi i t}$.
options.why: You used the period of $e^{it}$. Here $t$ counts whole turns, so the kernel is $\mathbb{Z}$.

hints.text: Read each row as: domain over kernel matches image.
The det row: the image is all non-zero reals.
$t \mapsto e^{2\pi i t}$ is 1 exactly at whole numbers $t$.

feedback.correct: Right. Four quotients, each read off a kernel and an image.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each map, divide the domain by the kernel and match it to the image.

byKey.detsign: You took the image of $\det$ as $\{1, -1\}$. Every non-zero real is a determinant.

explain.text: Each quotient is the domain over the kernel, matched to the image. So $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \cong \mathbb{Z}_n$ and $S_n/A_n \cong \{1, -1\}$, giving $|A_n| = n!/2$. The circle is $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ because $e^{2\pi i t} = 1$ exactly at whole numbers.

screens.title: Same size, same group?
screens.prose: $D_4/\langle r \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}_2$, from the two cosets of l11. A friend adds: $D_4/\{e, r^2\}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{12}/\langle 4 \rangle$ both have 4 elements, so they are isomorphic.
screens.question: Is the friend right?

options.text: No. $\mathbb{Z}_{12}/\langle 4 \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}_4$ has an element of order 4; the other has none.
Yes. Groups with the same number of elements are isomorphic.
options.why: You matched by size. An isomorphism keeps orders of elements, and here they differ.

options.text: Yes. Both are quotients by a subgroup, so they match.
options.why: You matched by construction. The subgroups and the groups differ, so the quotients can too.
You took $D_4/\langle r \rangle$. The quotient by $\{e, r^2\}$ has $8 / 2 = 4$ elements.

hints.text: An isomorphism sends an element of order 4 to one of order 4.
$1 + \langle 4 \rangle$ has order 4 (l11).
In $D_4/\{e, r^2\}$ every coset squares to the identity.

feedback.correct: Right. Size alone does not fix a group.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the orders of elements in the two groups.

byKey.yes: You took the size as enough. $\mathbb{Z}_4$ and the Klein four-group both have 4 elements and differ.

explain.text: An isomorphism keeps the order of every element. $\mathbb{Z}_4$ has an element of order 4, and the Klein four-group does not. So the two quotients are not isomorphic.

screens.title: Step 2: well defined
screens.prose: Write $K = \ker\varphi$, normal by l11. A coset has many names, so $\psi(gK) = \varphi(g)$ must give the same answer for each. Show it does. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose $gK = g'K$ (two names for one coset).
Then $g^{-1}g' \in K$ (l6: $g' = gk$ for some $k \in K$).
So $\varphi(g) = \varphi(g')$, and $\psi(gK)$ does not depend on the name (multiply by $\varphi(g)$).

lines.why: You treated a coset as having one name. $g$ and $g'$ may differ by any element of $K$.

hints.text: Turn $gK = g'K$ into a statement about $g^{-1}g'$.
$g^{-1}g'$ is in the kernel, so $\varphi$ sends it to $e$.
Split $\varphi(g^{-1}g')$ with the homomorphism rule.

feedback.correct: Right. Two names differ by a kernel element, which $\varphi$ ignores.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from $g^{-1}g' \in K$.

byKey.d1: You let a coset have one name. In $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$, $1 + K$ and $5 + K$ are the same coset.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: $gK = g'K$ means $g^{-1}g' \in K$. Then $\varphi(g)^{-1}\varphi(g') = e$, so $\varphi(g) = \varphi(g')$. The value of $\psi$ is the same for every name.

screens.title: Step 3: a homomorphism
screens.prose: The chain is $\psi(gK \cdot g'K) = \psi(gg'K) = \varphi(gg') = \varphi(g)\varphi(g') = \psi(gK)\psi(g'K)$. The first step is the coset product of l11.
screens.question: Which fact justifies $\varphi(gg') = \varphi(g)\varphi(g')$?

options.why: You picked normality. It made $gK \cdot g'K = gg'K$, the first step. This step is about $\varphi$.
You reached for a later step. Injectivity of $\psi$ plays no part in this equation.
You assumed $\varphi$ is onto. It need not be; that is why the target is $\operatorname{im}\varphi$.

hints.text: Which map appears on both sides?
The equation is about $\varphi$ alone.
$\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$ is the definition of a homomorphism.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the property of $\varphi$ that splits a product.

explain.text: $\varphi(gg') = \varphi(g)\varphi(g')$ is the homomorphism rule. So $\psi$ keeps the operation of $G/K$. Normality was used one step earlier.

screens.title: Step 4: injective
screens.prose: By l10, $\psi$ is injective when its kernel is just the identity coset $K$. One line below is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.why: That needs $\ker\varphi = \{e\}$. Here $g$ can be any element of $K$, and its coset is still $K$.

hints.text: Start from $\psi(gK) = e$.
Unwrap $\psi$: $\varphi(g) = e$.
So $g \in K$, and the coset $gK$ is $K$ itself.

feedback.correct: Right. Only the identity coset goes to $e$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Show that $\psi(gK) = e$ forces $gK = K$.

byKey.d1: You concluded $g = e$. Any $g \in K$ works, and every such $g$ gives the coset $K$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: $\psi(gK) = e$ means $\varphi(g) = e$, so $g \in K$. Then $gK = K$, the identity coset. So $\psi$ has trivial kernel and is injective.

screens.title: The whole proof
screens.prose: Put the steps together. Onto is free: every $\varphi(g)$ is $\psi(gK)$. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Order the proof that $G/\ker\varphi \cong \operatorname{im}\varphi$.

lines.text: Let $K = \ker\varphi$; $K$ is normal, so $G/K$ is a group (l11).
If $gK = g'K$ then $g^{-1}g' \in K$, so $\varphi(g) = \varphi(g')$: $\psi$ is well defined.
If $\psi(gK) = e$ then $g \in K$, so $gK = K$: $\psi$ is injective (l10).

lines.why: $\varphi$ need not be injective: $3x$ on $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ sends 0, 4 and 8 to 0. Injectivity of $\psi$ comes from the kernel test.

hints.text: Group first, then the map, then its three properties.
Well defined must come before anything else about $\psi$.
Order: normal, define, well defined, homomorphism, injective, onto, conclude.

feedback.correct: Right. That is the first isomorphism theorem.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Define $\psi$, check it is well defined, then prove it is a bijective homomorphism.

byKey.d1: You assumed $\varphi$ is injective. The theorem is for any homomorphism; injectivity of $\psi$ comes from dividing out $K$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: Normality makes $G/K$ a group, and well-definedness makes $\psi$ a function. Then $\psi$ is a homomorphism, injective by the kernel test and onto by construction. So $G/\ker\varphi \cong \operatorname{im}\varphi$.

screens.title: Spot the gap
screens.prose: A student hands in this proof. Every line is true, but one line claims something the proof never checks.

rows: 2. Define $\psi(gK) = \varphi(g)$; this is a map on cosets.
4. $\psi(gK) = e$ gives $g \in K$ and $gK = K$: injective.
5. $\psi$ hits every $\varphi(g)$, so it is onto $\operatorname{im}\varphi$.

screens.question: Tap the line with the gap.

hints.text: Which line would fail for $x \mapsto x \bmod 4$ on $\mathbb{Z}_6$ (l10)?
Defining a rule on cosets needs a check.
Line 2 never shows that two names of one coset give one value.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a definition that is used before it is checked.

byKey.r2: Line 3 is the homomorphism step, and it is sound once $\psi$ is a function.
byKey.r3: Line 4 is the kernel test of l10, and it is sound.
byKey.r0: Line 1 is sound: kernels are normal (l11).
byKey.r4: Line 5 is sound: onto holds by construction.

explain.text: Line 2 defines $\psi$ on cosets through a chosen name $g$. It must show that $gK = g'K$ gives $\varphi(g) = \varphi(g')$. Without that check, $\psi$ may not be a function at all.

screens.title: Modulo bias
screens.prose: A generator gives a uniform $x$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{16}$. Taking $x \bmod 8$ is a surjective homomorphism, so each residue is hit by a coset of size $16 / 8 = 2$. But $x \bmod 6$ is not a homomorphism from $\mathbb{Z}_{16}$, since 6 does not divide 16. Count how often each residue appears.
screens.question: For $x = 0$ to $15$, how many give each value of $x \bmod 6$?

hints.text: List 0 to 15 and reduce each modulo 6.
0, 6 and 12 give 0; 4 and 10 give 4.
Residues 0 to 3 appear three times, and 4 and 5 twice.

feedback.correct: Right. 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2: small residues come up more often.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the numbers from 0 to 15 with each remainder.

byKey.r4c1: Only 4 and 10 leave remainder 4; 16 is outside the range.

explain.text: Sixteen inputs do not split evenly into six residues. Residues 0 to 3 get three inputs and 4 and 5 get two. A die simulated as `rand() % 6` carries the same bias, much diluted.

ideas: Each value of a homomorphism is hit by one coset of the kernel, so $G/\ker\varphi \cong \operatorname{im}\varphi$ by $\psi(gK) = \varphi(g)$.
The proof: $K$ is normal and $\psi$ is well defined. Then $\psi$ is a homomorphism, injective by the kernel test, and onto.
For finite $G$, $|G| = |\ker\varphi| \cdot |\operatorname{im}\varphi|$, the group form of rank-nullity.
summary.trap: Defining $\psi(gK) = \varphi(g)$ without checking that every name of a coset gives the same value. And same size does not mean isomorphic.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide $|\mu_{12}| = 12$ by the size of the kernel.

byKey.kernel: You gave the size of the kernel. The quotient has $12 / 4$ cosets.

explain.text: $|\mu_{12}| = |\mu_4| \cdot |\mu_{12}/\mu_4|$, so the quotient has $12 / 4 = 3$ elements. It matches the image $\mu_3$. The count $12 = 4 \times 3$ is $|G| = |\ker\varphi| \cdot |\operatorname{im}\varphi|$.

quiz.prose: A 32-bit generator gives a uniform $x$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{2^{32}}$, and a die is simulated as $x \bmod 6$. Residues $0$ to $r - 1$ occur once more than the rest, where $r = 2^{32} \bmod 6$.
quiz.question: What is $2^{32} \bmod 6$?

feedback.correct: Right. Residues 0 to 3 occur 715,827,883 times and 4 and 5 occur 715,827,882 times.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Powers of 2 modulo 6 run 2, 4, 2, 4.

byKey.two: You took the odd powers' value. $2^{32}$ is an even power, and even powers of 2 are $4 \bmod 6$.

explain.text: Powers of 2 modulo 6 alternate 2, 4, so $2^{32} \equiv 4$. Then $2^{32} = 6 \times 715{,}827{,}882 + 4$. Residues 0 to 3 get one extra hit: a bias of about one in 715 million.

quiz.prose: Let $\varphi : G \to H$ be an injective homomorphism.
quiz.question: What does the theorem say?

options.why: You assumed $\varphi$ is onto $H$. It is onto its image only.
You used the trivial map's kernel. An injective map has kernel $\{e\}$, not $G$.

options.text: Nothing, since the theorem needs a non-trivial kernel.
options.why: The theorem holds for every homomorphism, trivial kernel included.

feedback.correct: Right. An injective homomorphism is an isomorphism onto its image.

explain.text: Injective means $\ker\varphi = \{e\}$, and $G/\{e\} \cong G$. So $G \cong \operatorname{im}\varphi$. At the other end, the trivial map has kernel $G$ and gives $G/G \cong \{e\}$.

quiz.prose: On the last screen, $x \bmod 6$ on $\mathbb{Z}_{16}$ gave counts 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2.
quiz.question: Why is $x \bmod 6$ not a homomorphism from $\mathbb{Z}_{16}$ to $\mathbb{Z}_6$?

options.text: 6 does not divide 16: $15 + 1 = 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{16}$, but $3 + 1 = 4$ in $\mathbb{Z}_6$.

options.why: It does hit all six residues. Onto is not the issue; the sums are.

options.text: It is a homomorphism; the unequal counts come from rounding.
options.why: You blamed rounding. A homomorphism has equal fibres, the cosets of its kernel, so unequal counts rule it out.
$0 \bmod 6 = 0$, so the identity test passes. The failure is at a wrap-around sum.

feedback.correct: Right. The wrap-around at 16 does not match the wrap-around at 6.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test a sum that wraps round in $\mathbb{Z}_{16}$.

explain.text: In $\mathbb{Z}_{16}$, $15 + 1 = 0$, which goes to 0. But $15 \bmod 6 + 1 \bmod 6 = 3 + 1 = 4$. A homomorphism would also give equal fibres, which the counts 3 and 2 rule out.
